newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA CENT.BANK ACTION UNLIKELY TO STOP LEU FALL.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA CENT.BANK ACTION UNLIKELY TO STOP LEU FALL.

text.p: Romania's leu currency, depressed to half its New Year rate against the dollar, held its ground on Thursday after central bank intervention, but traders predicted a resumption of its slide.

Dealers displayed interbank quotes at the end of trading in a range from 7,050 to 8,250, broadly unchanged from its opening and Wednesday's close after the central bank sold several million dollars. Before the intervention, the leu had opened weaker at a broad range of 8,250 to 8,950.

But dealers said most of Thursday's trading was at the bottom end of the range. They said the central bank had provided only a temporary reprieve despite a series of moves to tighten monetary policy, including large interest rate leaps.
"It appears the market has already swallowed the BNR dollars," one dealer said.
"Trading at 8,200/300 was more intense by the end of the day and this makes me believe the leu will weaken and the situation will go back to square one."
The leu, kept artificially high through most of last year by the leftist government before its November general election defeat, started the year at about 4,100.

The new centrist government under Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea has promoted tough monetary policy as a cornerstone of reforms to stabilise the economy, speed up privatisation and restructure bloated industry.

The government's plans, drawn up with the blessing of Western lenders, seek to cut inflation to 2.2 percent monthly by the year end from last month's 13.7 percent. The budget deficit is to be reduced to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from last year's 5.8 percent.
The central bank has declined all comment on its Wednesday intervention. Dealers said "several million dollars" were sold.

A central bank auction of one-week refinancing credits pushed up the average rate to 426.50 percent from 226.35 percent last week -- part of its strategy to create "leu hunger" and restore confidence in the currency.

The leaps have sent consumers scurrying to bank offices and currency shops to swap hoarded dollars for the leu to take advantage of higher deposit rates. But experts said this was unlikely to stave off further decline.
"Such a high jump in the one-week rate only gives you the feeling of risk looming ahead," one dealer said. "Most people will simply go back to the dollar and the leu will fall."
